To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
long‐term monoculturing (LTM) of soybean assembled the rhizosphere microbial community to suppress the soybean cyst (SCN) nematode, which has been the most destructive pathogen to this crop.
soybean‐monopoly cropping assembles the rhizosphere microbial community for the soil suppression to the soybean‐cyst nematode.
soybean monoculturing assembles a unique microbial community in the rhizospheres of soybean plants for the soil suppressiveness against Heterodera glycinis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the rhizosphere community assembly and its relationship to the soil suppressiveness of H. glycines.
the rhizosphere bacterial and fungal community assembly and its association with soil suppressiveness to SCN under LTM cropping in soybean.
how monoculture cropping of soybean assembles a specific rhizosphere microbiology for the suppression of Heteroderma glycines.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
monoculture of soybean in the long term (LTM) can engage exclusive bacterial and fungal communities to the rhizosphere that suppress the soybean cyst (SCN; nematode Heterodera glyces).
LTM cropping engaged exclusive bacterial and fungi taxa in the rhizo‐sphere microbiome for the soil suppression against SCN.

monoculturing of soybeans for long‐term (LTM) or short‐term (STM) durations in soils of northeastern China assembled exclusive bacterial and fungal species in the rhizospheres of the plants for the suppression of Heteroderaglycines.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
long‐term monoculturing of soybean engaged exclusive bacterial and functional fungal taxa in the soil suppressiveness to soybean cyst nemetode.
the rhizosphere microbial community is a key player in the long‐term suppression of SCN.
the rhizosphere of LTM cropping soybean assembled an exclusive microbiome for the soil suppression to H. glycines.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the microbial community in the rhizospheres of long‐term monocultured soils is distinct from that of soils under short‐term monoculturing, with the former showing higher relative abundance of bacterial and fungal taxa that are known to suppress H. glycines.
the rhizosphere microbial community is assembled in a manner that is conducive for soil suppressiveness of H. glycines.
long‐term monoculturing can shape the rhizosphere microbial community for disease suppression.
